blocks.content: Ladakh's Tibetan Buddhist monastic heritage is its single most internationally recognised cultural asset — this chapter catalogues the major monasteries ('gompas') by name, alongside the region's festival calendar and other cultural traditions.

cells: The largest and wealthiest monastery in Ladakh, belonging to the Drukpa Kagyu school; famous for the annual Hemis Festival (Chapter 10 below) commemorating Guru Padmasambhava
A striking, multi-storey monastery complex often compared architecturally to Tibet's Potala Palace; belongs to the Gelug school; houses a large seated Maitreya Buddha statue

One of Ladakh's oldest monastic complexes, renowned for exceptionally well-preserved 11th-century wall paintings and wood carvings, reflecting strong Kashmiri artistic influence from the monastery's early period
The oldest and largest monastery in the Nubra Valley, notable for its large modern statue of Maitreya Buddha overlooking the valley
One of Ladakh's oldest monasteries, set amid a strikingly eroded 'moonland' landscape formation
Belongs to the Gelug school; hosts the Spituk Gustor festival
Former summer palace/monastery complex of the Namgyal dynasty (Chapter 3), notable for a large seated Buddha statue

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Hemis Monastery — the largest/wealthiest in Ladakh — and Thiksey Monastery — the one most visually compared to the Potala Palace — are the two single most frequently tested monastery names; make sure not to swap these two specific superlatives.

cells: Commemorates the birth anniversary of Guru Padmasambhava; features elaborate masked 'Cham' dances performed by monks; held once every 12 years in an especially grand form
Ladakh's principal Buddhist New Year festival, marked by prayers, feasting and cultural performances across the region's Buddhist communities
A modern (since 1980s), UT-administration-promoted cultural festival showcasing Ladakhi music, dance, archery and polo, aimed at extending the tourist season into the shoulder months
Summer, near Leh (on the banks of the Indus)
A relatively modern festival celebrating the Indus River's cultural and civilisational significance, drawing participants from across India
Masked Cham dance festivals held at specific monasteries (e.g., Spituk Gustor, Tsemo Gustor), each with locally specific timing and ritual significance

items: Ladakhi cuisine draws heavily on Tibetan culinary tradition, with staples including 'thukpa' (noodle soup), 'momos' (dumplings), 'skyu' (a traditional pasta-and-vegetable stew), butter tea ('gur gur chai'), and barley-based 'tsampa' (roasted barley flour), reflecting the region's high-altitude, limited-agriculture dietary adaptations.

Traditional Ladakhi architecture — flat-roofed, whitewashed stone/mud-brick houses, and the distinctive monastery/gompa architectural style — is well adapted to the region's cold, dry, seismically-moderate climate.

Polo has a particularly deep traditional association with Ladakh (and the wider Baltistan/Gilgit region), historically considered one of the sport's ancestral homelands in the Indian subcontinent, alongside archery as another traditionally significant sport, both showcased at the modern Ladakh Festival.

Thangka painting (traditional Tibetan Buddhist scroll painting) and Pashmina weaving (linked to the Changthang wool-production economy, Chapter 8) are among Ladakh's most significant traditional visual-arts and craft traditions.
Hemis Monastery = largest/wealthiest in Ladakh (Drukpa Kagyu school); Thiksey Monastery = most Potala-Palace-like in appearance (Gelug school).
Alchi Monastery: one of Ladakh's oldest, famous for 11th-century wall paintings showing strong Kashmiri artistic influence.
Hemis Festival commemorates Guru Padmasambhava's birth, with masked 'Cham' dances; Losar = Ladakhi Buddhist New Year.
Ladakh Festival (autumn, Leh) is a modern government-promoted cultural showcase; Sindhu Darshan Festival celebrates the Indus River.
Polo and archery have deep traditional roots in Ladakh; Thangka painting and Pashmina weaving are key craft traditions.
